document.title: Protest of Microsoft Corporation re American Transmission Company LLC's 08/17/2026 tariff filing

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
American Transmission Company LLC; 
Midcontinent Independent System 
Operator, Inc. 
) 
) 
) 
Docket No. ER26-3531-000 
 
 
 
PROTEST OF MICROSOFT CORPORATION 
 
 
Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission’s”) 
Combined Notice of Filings #1,1 Microsoft Corporation (“Microsoft”) respectfully submits 
for the Commission’s consideration these comments on the August 17, 2026 filing of 
Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”), on behalf of American 
Transmission Company LLC (“ATC”).2 ATC is one of two MISO utilities that retains local 
transmission planning responsibilities, with those planning procedures set out in Attachment 
FF-ATCLLC of MISO’s Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating Reserve Markets 
Tariff (“Tariff”).3 ATC intends the proposed reforms in this docket to comply with the local 
transmission planning obligations directed by the Commission in the MISO Show Cause 
Order4 and to complement MISO’s to-be-filed tariff reforms in compliance with that order.5  
Microsoft supports transparent, durable, and nondiscriminatory local transmission 
planning processes necessary for interconnection and reliable service to transmission 
 
1 Combined Notice of Filings #1, Docket No. ER26-3531-000 (Aug. 17, 2026). 
2 Am. Trans. Co. LLC, Proposed Revisions to Attachment FF-ATCLLC of the MISO Tariff in 
Response to Show Cause Order, Docket No. ER26-3531-000 (Aug. 17, 2026) (“ATC Filing”). 
3 MISO performs local planning services for all but two of its transmission-owning members.  
4 Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Op., Inc., Order Instituting Proceeding under Section 206 of the 
Federal Power Act, 195 FERC ¶ 61,212 (2026) (“Show Cause Order”). 
5 August 17 Filing at 1 (“ATC is proposing certain revisions . . . to fulfill obligations outlined 
in the Show Cause Order”).

2 
 
customers on behalf of their large retail loads. As Microsoft explained in a related ATC 
proceeding,6 as a signatory to the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge, Microsoft is 
fully committed to “pay for all new power delivery infrastructure upgrades required to 
service [] data centers, including adequate network upgrade costs to ensure that these 
expenses are not passed on to the ordinary household.”7 In this case, however, Microsoft is 
concerned that ATC’s proposed local planning reforms do not align with the longstanding 
planning principles of Order No. 890 and fall short of reforms contemplated by the 
Commission in the Show Cause Order for three primary reasons: 
1. ATC’s proposed local planning reforms do not give stakeholders like Microsoft a 
meaningful role, or even opportunity, to provide input into the planning process, even 
though this process will determine the facilities, schedule, and cost for which the 
applicable large retail customer is ultimately liable.   
 
2. The proposed local planning reforms expand ATC’s unilateral exercise of discretion 
without guardrails and may produce inconsistent and unduly preferential or 
discriminatory outcomes that have consequences under the Federal Power Act.   
 
3. The proposed local planning reforms require ATC to enter into two different contracts 
with its customers, but ATC has not filed these contracts as pro forma—nor has it 
explained why not.8  
 
If ATC’s objective is to provide the same treatment to all transmission customers with large 
loads, ATC has not explained why it omitted pro forma contracts and will be instead 
negotiating those agreements separately for each of its transmission customer’s new large 
 
6 Am. Trans. Co. LLC; Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Op., Inc., Protest and Motion for Hearing 
and Settlement Judge Procedures of Microsoft Corp. at 2, Docket No. ER26-3265-000 (filed Aug. 21, 
2026). 
7 Ratepayer Protection Pledge at P 2, available at 
https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/03/ratepayer-protection-pledge/ 
8 The contracts are not part of the record in this docket. ATC has not provided them, even for 
informational purposes.

3 
 
loads. Moreover, ATC has not shown its reforms to comply fully with the longstanding 
planning principles of Order No. 890.9   
Access to reliable electric service is essential to expand the capacity of cloud 
computing and artificial intelligence data center sectors, and observance of longstanding, 
proven utility regulatory principles like open access support the competitive, responsible 
growth that is necessary for U.S. leadership in the computing industry. If the Commission 
does not reject the ATC Filing, Microsoft requests that the Commission initiate 
unconsolidated hearing and settlement judge procedures in this proceeding and in the Docket 
No. ER26-3265-000 proceeding so that Microsoft and other interested stakeholders may 
work with ATC to resolve deficiencies in its local transmission planning processes.       
I. 
PROTEST 
A. 
ATC’s local planning reforms to address large load interconnection and 
service exclude participation by large retail customers like Microsoft.   
As noted above, ATC is one of two transmission-owning members of MISO that 
retain authority over local transmission planning instead of delegating that responsibility to 
the grid operator. Accordingly, ATC performs local transmission planning pursuant to 
Attachment FF-ATCLLC of the MISO Tariff.10 As described in Attachment FF-ATCLLC, 
ATC administers the process for distribution-transmission interconnection planning, which 
involves planning for interconnection and service to distribution utilities, among other local 
 
9 Preventing Undue Discrimination and Preference in Transmission Service, Order No. 890, 
118 FERC ¶ 61,119 (Feb. 16, 2007) (“Order No. 890”); see also Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Op., Inc. 
and Am. Trans. Co. LLC., Revisions to Attachment FF-ATCLLC of the Midwest ISO Open Access 
Transmission and Energy Markets Tariff, Docket No. OA08-42-000 (filed Dec. 7, 2007).  
10 ATC is not permitted by state law to delegate its local transmission planning authority to 
MISO or any other entity. See ATC Filing at 2, nn.7, 9.

4 
 
planning responsibilities. The proposed large load-related changes include adding to 
Attachment FF-ATCLLC newly defined terms like ATCLLC Large Load, Large Load 
Interconnection Criteria Confirmation Form, Load Interconnection Request Form, and 
ATCLLC Local Planning Criteria.11 The changes specifically address interconnection and 
service to distribution utilities for loads that are equal to or exceed 100 MW, and by 
extension are intended to capture the new loads of large retail customers like Microsoft.   
Microsoft has been working collaboratively with ATC and Wisconsin Electric Power 
Company, dba We Energies (“WEPCo”) to interconnect and serve Microsoft’s large data 
center campus in Racine County, Wisconsin. Microsoft appreciates ATC’s efforts to support 
the reliable integration of large retail loads into the transmission system and recognizes that a 
large retail load like a data center may have a significant grid impact.  
As a retail customer, Microsoft also recognizes the degree of separation that exists 
between it and ATC; however, Microsoft respectfully submits that large retail customers are 
important stakeholders in ATC’s local transmission planning work. As the Commission 
recognized in the Show Cause Order, stakeholder engagement is part of the tariff revision 
process.12  The most significant consequence of ATC developing these reforms without 
broad stakeholder consultation is that the proposed local planning procedures appear to 
exclude the opportunity for participation by interested large retail customers like Microsoft. 
Microsoft respectfully submits that local transmission planning processes should give large 
retail customers the option to participate—for instance, to test and validate local transmission 
 
11 The Large Load Interconnection Criteria Confirmation Form, Load Interconnection 
Request Form, and ATCLLC Local Planning Criteria are not part of Attachment FF-ATCLLC. 
Section I.C addresses Microsoft’s concerns that certain agreements referenced in the local planning 
procedures are not tariffed pro forma agreements. 
12 See, e.g., Show Cause Order at PP 37, 41, 53, 62, 71, 73-76, 84

5 
 
needs, to explore solutions to challenges, to support the utility’s consideration of grid-
enhancing technologies, or to coordinate on load ramp and in-service timelines. Retail 
customers’ participation in federally regulated electric matters is not a new concept at all, as 
the Commission has previously found that end-use retail customers may participate in the 
formula rate protocol process.13 
ATC’s proposed reforms to its local planning process, however, do not contemplate 
that approach. For example, ATC provides for an “annual process to re-evaluate the 
ATCLLC Local Planning Criteria and requirements established by ATCLLC’s Business 
Practices to ensure the ATCLLC Local Planning Criteria and requirements established by 
ATCLLC’s Business Practices appropriately meet all requirements described herein.”14 
Changes coming out of that process would now become effective “immediately following” 
the posting of the revisions (instead of 30 days after posting as the currently effective Order 
No. 890-approved procedures provide).15 The tariff reforms do not contemplate the 
participation of large retail loads in the annual review process. In Microsoft’s view, ATC 
should provide interested stakeholders with notice of the annual review process (such as by 
 
13 See, e.g., See Am. Elec. Power Serv. Corp., 153 FERC ¶ 61,167 at P 12 (2015) (“As 
explained below, the Commission concludes that: (1) retail ratepayers may file complaints and protest 
transmission rates and wholesale power sales rates before the Commission; and (2) allowing retail 
customers to challenge transmission and wholesale power sales rates does not violate principles of 
federalism.”). See also id. at P 19 (“As the Commission found in PATH, indirect customers (e.g., 
retail customers) have a right to intervene and protest rates when some portion of those rates will be 
flowed through to their retail bill. Ms. Peine has, in fact, intervened in this matter and protested the 
SWEPCO/AEP Annual Update filings and, therefore, we see no reason to treat her participation any 
differently than the retail customers in PATH who similarly protested the formula rate updates, but 
did not intervene.”). 
14 Attachment FF-ATCLLCA, § V.F. 
15Id.

6 
 
posting on OASIS) and the tariff should provide a meaningful opportunity for large retail 
customers and other stakeholders to engage with ATC and stress-test proposed changes.  
With regard to ATC’s process for requesting transmission-distribution 
interconnection to serve the large load of a distribution utility, such as WEPCo’s service to 
Microsoft’s Racine County data center campus, the tariff procedures should permit the large 
retail customer to participate in Distribution Interconnection Planning Meetings and to access 
transmission data and planning models. ATC holds distribution interconnection planning 
meetings only with “individual owners of Distribution Facilities”; it does not include the 
retail customers even though the purpose of these meetings is to 
provide an opportunity for [ATC] to obtain such other information, or to 
validate previously received information, and to discuss with such 
Distribution Facility owners whether the studies or assessments then being 
performed or which are to be performed, are appropriate to meet their 
respective needs, and to determine whether the study models or assessment 
tools are appropriate for the particular Distribution Interconnection or 
Distribution Facilities owner’s requirements.16 
A large retail customer could contribute meaningfully to these planning discussions. At the 
bare minimum, the large retail customer should be provided with the “results of [ATC’s] 
study or assessment” and ATC should have the opportunity to receive the large retail 
customer’s comments on the study.17  
If ATC’s local planning procedures were reformed to provide a large retail customer 
with the opportunity to participate, it would be reasonable to provide a large retail load 
access to the same dispute resolution process available to ATC and its distribution utility. 
ATC’s local planning procedures direct that any dispute in connection with a distribution 
 
16 Id. § VI.A.7. 
17Id. § VI.A.8.

7 
 
interconnection request “shall be handled” in accordance with the process specified in a 
Distribution-Transmission Interconnection Agreement between ATC and the distribution 
utility.18 Although a large retail customer is ultimately responsible for the costs of facilities 
developed during the local planning process,19 even with the large load reforms proposed by 
ATC in this docket there is not yet an opportunity for that customer to resolve concerns 
quickly and efficiently through a tariffed alternative dispute resolution process such as the 
process directed under Order No. 890’s dispute resolution planning principle.20 Instead, the 
only option available to a large retail customer is to file a section 206 complaint with the 
Commission. To the extent the Commission intended its Show Cause Order reforms to 
provide large retail customers with the opportunity for direct engagement, the local planning 
reforms proposed in this docket do not achieve that objective. 
B. 
ATC’s local planning reforms provide ATC with substantial discretion 
and creates risk of undue discrimination and preferential treatment to 
similarly situated transmission customers.  
Order No. 890 required transmission providers to adopt transmission planning 
processes that are coordinated, open, transparent, and comparable because planning decisions 
can materially affect access to transmission service, project timing, facility requirements, and 
 
18 Id. § VII.C (disputes arising in connection with distribution interconnection requests). 
19 E.g., Am. Trans. Co. LLC, Comments of the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin at 5, 
Docket No. ER26-3265-000 (Aug. 14, 2026). 
20 Nothing in Order No. 890 suggests that the alternative dispute resolution process may 
foreclose participation of a large retail customer. To the contrary, FERC “encourage[d] transmission 
providers, customers, and other stakeholders” to utilize Commission resources in developing a 
tariffed dispute resolution processes. Order No. 890 at P 503; see id. at PP 496-503. See also Order 
No. 890-A, 121 FERC ¶ 61,297 at PP 217-21 (Dec. 28, 2007); see id. at P 220 (“Any stakeholder that 
has concerns regarding the dispute resolution mechanism proposed by a transmission provider, or any 
other aspect of the compliance filing, may bring them to the Commission’s attention on review of the 
proposal.”).

8 
 
cost.21 The Commission further recognized in that rulemaking that transmission customers 
and other stakeholders must have a meaningful opportunity to participate in the planning 
process and that planning standards must be sufficiently transparent to permit customers to 
understand and evaluate planning outcomes.  
Since its Order No. 890 compliance docket more than two decades ago, ATC’s local 
planning procedures have remained largely unchanged.22 Here, however, ATC wants to 
loosen practices with new grants of discretion, undefined readiness requirements, extra-tariff 
criteria and business practices, discretionary access to its planning models, and to determine 
what studies, facilities, and upgrades are “necessary” or “appropriate.”23 Nowhere in 
Attachment FF-ATCLLC are readiness requirements actually specified, even though a 
distribution customer’s ability to “meet” or “complete” “all applicable readiness 
requirements” is required to proceed through the local planning process.24 These deficiencies 
weaken the coordinated, open and transparent transmission planning framework developed 
under Order No. 890 and increase the likelihood of unduly preferential and discriminatory 
treatment of transmission customers and, as follows, their large retail customers. For 
instance:     
• Any interested party may request, in writing, copies of the models developed using 
the assessment tools employed by ATCLLC in performing any planning function or 
associated analysis or assessment, and ATCLLC may, in its discretion provide copies 
 
21 See, e.g., Order No. 890 at PP 451-54, 460, 471-79; see also id. at P 488 (“The 
transmission planning required by this Final Rule is intended to provide transmission customers and 
other stakeholders a meaningful opportunity to engage in planning along with their transmission 
providers.”). 
22 See generally Docket No. OA08-42-000 et al. 
23 E.g., Attachment FF-ATCLLC, §§ III, V.E─V.G., VI.A.2, VI.A.6─VI.A.7, 
VI.A.10─VI.A.12, VI.B.3─VI.B.4, VI.B.7, VI.C.2, VI.C.4─VI.V.5. 
24Id. § VI.A.4.

9 
 
of such models under appropriate confidentiality agreements, subject to the rules and 
regulations of the FERC.”25 
• “Distribution –Transmission Interconnection Requests are studied or assessed by 
ATCLLC primarily upon a first come, first served basis upon completion of any 
applicable readiness requirements.”26 “Each request is studied in the order in which 
such request meets applicable readiness requirements, unless in ATCLLC’s judgment 
and determination, require that a later received request should be studied prior to 
earlier received requests.”27 
• “The terms and conditions of the Distribution – Transmission Interconnection 
Agreement published on ATCLLC’s website may be changed, modified or revised 
by ATCLLC in its judgment and determination….”28 
• “The ATCLLC Local Planning Criteria and requirements established by ATCLLC’s 
Business Practices may be revised from time to time in response to changes in 
industry standards, new system conditions, new technologies and new operating 
procedures, as appropriate and subject to change at any time at ATC’s discretion.”29  
• “Change, modification, supplement, or revision to the ATCLLC Local Planning 
Criteria and/or requirements established by ATCLLC’s Business Practices shall 
become applicable immediately following the posting by ATCLLC of such revised 
criteria to the ATCLLC website.”30 
• “ATCLLC shall reflect such modifications to existing Distribution Interconnections 
or proposed new Distribution Interconnections . . . and the Transmission Facilities 
that are determined to be necessary as a result of such study or studies or other 
assessment shall be incorporated into such other planning functions . . . to the extent 
necessary or appropriate to reflect the effect of such request or the Transmission 
Facilities determined necessary”31  
• “To the extent necessary and appropriate, ATCLLC shall incorporate the results of 
the studies or assessments performed for any and all Distribution – Transmission 
Interconnection Requests in its network assessment.”32   
 
25 Attachment FF-ATCLLCA, § V.G. 
26 Id. § VI.A.2. 
27Id. 
28 Id. § IV (definition of Distribution – Transmission Interconnection Agreement). 
29 Id. § V.F. 
30 Id. 
31 Id. § VI.A.11. 
32 Id.

10 
 
Microsoft recognizes that transmission providers and transmission owners must 
confront challenges today that are very different from those that existed when Order No. 890 
was issued nearly two decades ago. Microsoft also appreciates ATC’s work to reform its 
local transmission planning process to address the growing demand associated with large 
retail loads while maintaining system reliability and preventing inappropriate cost shifts to 
other customers. As the Commission evaluates ATC’s proposed revisions to Attachment FF-
ATCLLC, however, Microsoft respectfully requests that it consider not only whether the 
proposal addresses the operational challenges posed by large-load interconnections, but also 
whether the proposal preserves the fundamental structural safeguards of open access 
transmission service.  
C. 
ATC’s local planning reforms exclude pro forma agreements although 
ATC requires the parties to execute these contracts, further 
exacerbating the risk of undue discrimination and preferential 
treatment. 
ATC’s proposal contemplates that transmission customers requesting transmission 
service for an ATCLLC Large Load will be required to enter into a Minimum Transmission 
Charge Agreement (“MTCA”) and one or more Large Load Project Commitment 
Agreements (“LLPCAs”). Microsoft protested these agreements for its Racine County data 
center campus submitted by ATC in currently pending Docket No. ER26-3265 because as-
filed, those agreements contained blatant errors and deficiencies, and raised cost-of-service 
and open access red flags. As in this proceeding, the agreements at issue in Docket No. 
ER26-3265 were negotiated without any input or participation from Microsoft, and the 
consequences of this fact are axiomatic in their structural shortcomings.   
Microsoft understands that ATC’s preference is that its transmission customers 
remain subject to the same terms and conditions. Yet Microsoft cannot reconcile this stated

11 
 
preference with ATC’s decision to omit the MTCA and the LLPCA as pro forma contracts in 
Attachment FF-ATCLLC. These agreements establish the substantive rights and obligations 
that will govern the planning, construction, financing, and operation of facilities necessary to 
serve large loads, and ultimately their terms will flow through to the large load retail 
customer. Their absence from the Tariff is significant. By requiring customers to enter into 
agreements that are not part of a generally applicable Tariff in order to receive electric 
service, ATC introduces a level of discretion that creates a substantial risk that similarly 
situated customers may be offered materially different terms and conditions. The danger is 
particularly acute when the agreements are negotiated exclusively between ATC and its 
affiliates (like WEPCo) without any input from the applicable large load customer, as is the 
case for the agreements currently pending in Docket No. ER26-3265. The Commission 
recognizes that pro forma contracts have a role in ensuring that transmission providers 
administer jurisdictional services on a transparent, consistent, and non-discriminatory basis. 
Recently, in PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., the Commission explained that where specific 
contractual provisions provide benefits to interconnection customers, those benefits should 
be made available through a pro forma agreement “to ensure that all similarly situated 
interconnection customers are treated on a consistent and fair basis.”33 Likewise, in 
Southwest Power Pool, Inc., the Commission reminded the grid operator that if it elects to 
offer a particular form of service, the applicable terms and benefits should be memorialized 
in a pro forma agreement “to ensure that all similarly-situated interconnection customers are 
treated on a consistent and fair basis.”34 These precedents  recognize the concerns here—
 
33 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 191 FERC ¶ 61,025, at P25 (2025). 
34 Sw. Power Pool Inc., 128 FERC ¶ 61,191, at P 21 (2009).

12 
 
transparency and comparability are undermined when contracts for a tariff service are 
negotiated outside of a generally applicable tariff framework. Because ATC intends the 
MTCA and the LLPCA to become a standard feature of local transmission planning and 
service, the terms governing those arrangements should be set in Commission-approved pro 
forma agreements rather than through individualized negotiations or website-posted contracts 
that may change over time. 
The Commission reached a similar conclusion in MidAmerican Energy Co., where it 
rejected non-conforming provisions in an interconnection agreement, explaining that the 
insurance requirements the transmission provider wished to adopt for one interconnection 
customer should instead be incorporated into the pro forma Large Generator Interconnection 
Agreement.35 The Commission emphasized there that pro forma agreements are necessary to 
ensure that all similarly situated customers are “treated on a consistent and fair basis.”36 That 
safeguard is particularly relevant here because the agreements contemplated by ATC will 
govern matters that may ultimately determine a large retail customer’s financial exposure, 
project development obligations, termination rights, security requirements, and long-term 
service costs. Without Commission-approved pro forma agreements, large retail customers 
have no assurance that these provisions will be applied consistently from one large project to 
the next.   
 
35 MidAmerican Energy Co., 116 FERC ¶ 61,018, at P 12 (2006) (“Indeed, MidAmerican’s 
proposed insurance requirements are tailored to more closely match the need for insurance with the 
exposure to liabilities by not requiring the full insurance coverage until construction commences.  
However, these benefits should be made available to all interconnection customers in a transparent, 
non-discriminatory manner so that MidAmerican cannot favor Pomeroy Wind over the rest of 
MidAmerican’s customers.”). 
36 Id.; See also Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 129 FERC ¶ 61,121, at P 13 (2009) (stating that “[t]he 
use of pro forma documents ensures that interconnection customers receive non-discriminatory 
service and that all interconnection customers are treated on a consistent and fair basis.”).

13 
 
ATC has not explained why it did not propose a pro forma MTCA and LLPCA to 
comply with the Show Cause Order, when pro forma contracts are consistent with 
longstanding Commission policy and precedent. Permitting ATC to require execution of non-
tariffed agreements while reserving discretion over their contents only exacerbates concerns 
regarding transparency, comparability, and the potential for inconsistent treatment by ATC 
among its customers. 
II. 
CONCLUSION 
Microsoft respectfully requests that the Commission initiate hearing and settlement 
judge procedures in this proceeding to allow Microsoft and other interested stakeholders to 
work with ATC to develop robust local planning procures. In the alternative, Microsoft 
respectfully requests that the Commission reject the proposed tariff changes without prejudice 
to be refiled. 
Respectfully submitted,
